rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zawj means a type, so the phrase describes many different kinds of beneficial things sprouted from the earth.
rows.anchor: various types of things.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term translated beneficial is associated with grapes, which Arabs named for their recognized benefits.
rows.anchor: means “being beneficial.” The Arabs generally called grapes as

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth's abundant blessings answer those waiting for a heavenly punishment sign; God created them so people benefit and take reminders.
rows.anchor: multifarious favours and blessings of God spread in the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth's blessings are a great sign, recalling the Qur'an's comprehensive proofs for monotheism and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: all the arguments that the Qur’ ān has comprehensively presented in favour of monotheism and the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs are plentiful everywhere on earth, but they cannot benefit people who refuse faith.
rows.anchor: each and every place on this earth has them; yet they can be of no use to those who do not want to accept faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's might means He can punish without anyone stopping or rescuing them; His mercy delays punishment so people can reform and earn mercy.
rows.anchor: Since He is powerful, He can do anything and no one can stop Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the inchoative stresses God's attributes and warns that people wrongly treat His respite as proof of their own truth, then mock reformers.
rows.anchor: The inchoative is repeated here to stress these attributes of God and direct the attention of people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated closing verses recur through the sūrah, so readers should understand their explanation here for later occurrences.
rows.anchor: these verses, as has been referred to earlier, will occur repeatedly in this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section recounts Shu‘ayb and the people of Madyan: as Lot warned about moral misconduct, Shu‘ayb warned about economic misconduct; they persisted and met the other nations' fate, and the account closes with repeated verses.
rows.anchor: Just as Lot (sws) warned his nation of their moral misconduct, Shu‘ayb (sws) warned his nation of economic misconduct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-aykah refers to bushes or forests; a forest near Madyan gave its residents the name People of the Forest.
rows.anchor: refers to bushes and forests. There was a forest near Madyan.

rows.speaker: Some exegetes
rows.claim: Some exegetes distinguish the People of Madyan from the People of the Forest and say Shu‘ayb was sent to both nations.
rows.anchor: Some exegetes think that the “People of Madyan” and the “People of the Forest” are different from one another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the view that the People of Madyan and the People of the Forest were separate nations.
rows.anchor: In my view, this opinion is incorrect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening verses repeat material from the preceding prophetic account and have already been explained.
rows.anchor: These verses occur in the previous anecdote and have already been explained.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan's people were accomplished traders, but indifference to God and the Hereafter let Satan turn their trade toward cheating in weights.
rows.anchor: The people of Madyan were traders by profession and had advanced to great heights in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fraudulent weighing is a contagious economic disease that pulls traders and businesses into wider deception and exploitation.
rows.anchor: This economic misconduct is a severe disease that is contagious.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the world depend on balance; it guides people to uphold justice throughout society and the economy, whose balance can otherwise collapse.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has created this world with a balance and the heavens and the earth remain intact because of this balance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Selling goods in a reduced or adulterated form is a particularly heinous way of shortchanging people.
rows.anchor: A very heinous form of selling goods to people by lessening them is adulteration.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adulteration dilutes goods such as wheat, oil, sugar, or milk with cheaper substances, leaving less of the real product even when the measured amount is correct.
rows.anchor: adding barley in wheat, fat in oil, sand in sugar, water in milk.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adulteration with harmful substances makes buyers unsure whether market food is poison or ordinary edible food.
rows.anchor: he is not even sure if he is gulping poison or some common edibles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If prosperity depends on destroying the balance, it is a curse rather than a benefit.
rows.anchor: if these people have advanced at the expense of destroying this balance, then such advancement is a bane not a boon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should act as reformers rather than spread disorder, and recognize the terrible consequence of earning through unlawful means.
rows.anchor: Their ways should be the ways of reformers and not of those who spread disorder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jabillah means creatures; Shu‘ayb reminds his people that their Creator is the same One who created earlier generations and punished their corruption.
rows.anchor: The word ﺟﺒﻠﺔٌ means “creatures.” Here, prophet Shu‘ayb (sws) has asked his people to learn a lesson from history.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Creator is the same, His treatment and law will not change: the people should fear Him, reform, and expect punishment for economic misconduct.
rows.anchor: They will be punished for their economic misconduct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu‘ayb's people answered with the standard taunt used by those who reject messengers, calling him bewitched, mortal, and a liar.
rows.anchor: an answer given by the rejecters of all messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kisf is the plural of kisfah.
rows.anchor: The wordﻛﺴْﻒٌ  is a plural of ﻛﺴْﻔﺔٌ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demand for pieces of the sky answered Shu‘ayb's warning that rejecting him would bring punishment like that of ‘Ād, Thamūd, and Lot's people.
rows.anchor: this demand put forth by his nation to send down pieces of the sky on them was made in response to his warning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu‘ayb entrusts the threatened punishment to God: its timing and form belong to God's wisdom, and God knows the people's conduct.
rows.anchor: dropping pieces from the sky was under God’s jurisdiction and not his.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description in al-A‘rāf is consistent with a stone-hurling wind; the canopy looked like a distant column of dust or smoke and included earthquake, shout, and canopy.
rows.anchor: the nature of this torment was that of a stone-hurling wind that has been referred to in the anecdote of prophet Lot (sws) as ḥāṣib.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Hūd 11:94 the torment is called a shout or thunder.
rows.anchor: which means shout and thunder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated closing verses have already been explained.
rows.anchor: These repetitive verses at the end have already been explained.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding discourse returns to the sūrah's opening theme: Qur'anic warnings are true, punishment signs can come, and prophetic histories already serve as signs for the stubborn Quraysh.
rows.anchor: Coming up are the concluding verses of the sūrah and the discourse links to its introductory part which is the real theme.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qaṣaṣ is the counterpart of al-Naml and shares its central theme; it expands Moses' story from birth through receiving the Torah, while now treating Israel's righteous and wicked elements openly.
rows.anchor: complete details of this account are mentioned, beginning from his birth to being given the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like Joseph's story in Sūrah Yūsuf, Moses' story lets Muhammad see God's protection of messengers and fulfillment of His plans, while warning opponents of their eventual fate.
rows.anchor: in the mirror of these tales, Mu ḥammad (sws) is able to fully observe how majestically the Almighty protects His messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account tells Quraysh that God sent Muhammad and this Book just as He sent Moses to Pharaoh, giving them guidance and leaving no excuse for their wrong ways.
rows.anchor: just as the Almighty had sent Moses (sws) as a Messenger to the Pharaoh and his people, in a similar way, He has sent this Messenger and this Book to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Muhammad was absent from Moses' events, his detailed knowledge demonstrates revelation; God revives lost guidance for Israelites through him and conclusively conveys truth.
rows.anchor: was absent at the time, it was not possible that he would have been able to know

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad did not ask for the Qur'an; God entrusted it to him, so he should fulfill his duty despite opposition, trusting God's help and success.
rows.anchor: The Prophet Mu ḥammad (sws) is assured that he has not demanded this Qur’ ān from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–43 recount Moses' life from birth until he receives the Torah.
rows.anchor: from his birth t ill the time he was given the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 44–46 turn to Muhammad's absence from Moses' story and God's favor in informing him, reviving the sharī‘ah through him, and warning Quraysh before punishment.
rows.anchor: God wanted to conclusively convey the truth to them through him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh opposed the call and, at Jewish prompting, demanded miracles like Moses'; the answer silences them and praises People of the Book who supported the Prophet.
rows.anchor: This demand was implanted in their minds by the Jews.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage reassures the Prophet and answers Quraysh's fear that accepting the call would destroy their political and economic influence.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is given assurance and an answer is given to the Quraysh to allay their fear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage exposes the baselessness of Quraysh's idols and intercessors, which they viewed as sources of success and feared abandoning.
rows.anchor: that if they left them, they would be destroyed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fate of a wealthy Jewish capitalist shows that God grants favors, though the wretched attribute them to their own ability and idols.
rows.anchor: The fate of a capitalist Jew is mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must remain steadfast and disregard opponents, relying on the God who entrusted him with spreading the Qur'an to help through difficulty.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is urged to remain steadfast on his stance and disregard his opponents.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The isolated letters were discussed earlier; the clear Book carries both favor and conclusive communication of truth, especially for the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: has in it the elements of both favour and

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar introduction in the preceding sūrah is clear evidence that both sūrahs share a central theme.
rows.anchor: The previous sūrah also has a very similar introductory verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although addressed to Muhammad, the verse's closing words warn Quraysh's leaders, Pharaohs of their own age.
rows.anchor: the last words are proof of the fact that the purpose of narrating this account is to sound a warning to the leaders of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bil-haqq means an exact and purposeful account that teaches; the Torah neither reports Moses and Pharaoh accurately nor conveys the story's real lesson, while the Qur'an does both.
rows.anchor: in truth, the way it exactly is with an objective and a purpose to teach a lesson.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about those who believe expresses intention and warns that only those intending faith benefit; the blind and deaf will not change.
rows.anchor: only those people will benefit from this account, narrated by God, who have the intention to profess faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before the story, these verses state its purpose, a Qur'anic technique that keeps readers focused; Sūrah al-Kahf provides another example.
rows.anchor: before narrating an account the message it is intended to convey is very concisely stated before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tyranny means ignoring the Creator's purpose and commands, following one's desires, and demanding that people worship and obey oneself instead of God.
rows.anchor: To be tyrannical in the land means that a person ignores the intent and directives of the real Creator of this universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh divided people into classes and enslaved a faction; since rulers and subjects are all God's servants, law, justice, and equality must apply alike to both.
rows.anchor: When the ruler and the ruled both are slaves of God, then it is not permissible for a ruler to discriminate between his subjects.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh enslaved the Israelites and claimed divine status, while authorizing the Copts to force them into labor.
rows.anchor: Yet the Pharaoh had made the Israelites his slaves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Slaughtering Israelite boys and sparing their women exemplified Pharaoh's oppression; the motive for the policy was explained in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: example of the oppression and injustice which the Pharaoh and the Copts had subjected the Israelites to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh spread disorder, although God grants power and authority to establish justice and peace on earth.
rows.anchor: power and authority for the sole reason of establishing justice and peace in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic syntax suppresses an incomplete verb before nurid; Pharaoh sought to keep Israel oppressed, while God intended to favor them, make them religious leaders, and let them rule after the oppressors' destruction.
rows.anchor: the Pharaoh and his companions were bent upon oppressing the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imamate denotes the Israelites' religious leadership after Moses, while inheritors refers to their political power in Palestine, greatly expanded under Solomon.
rows.anchor: religious authority which the Israelites were bestowed after the advent of Moses (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamkin means political power; God intended to give the oppressed a strong kingdom and show Pharaoh and Haman what they feared.
rows.anchor: means political authority and power. In other words, God intended

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh feared Israel's rising numbers and imagined they could seize Egypt or ally with outside enemies; his preventive plots could not defeat God's plan.
rows.anchor: they feared the ever increasing number of the Israelites.
